sections.overview: The thick-billed cuckoo is an African cuckoo distinguished by its unusually heavy bill. It is a specialized brood parasite of helmetshrikes, an uncommon host choice among cuckoos.
sections.identification: At about 36 cm long, it is a large, robust cuckoo with a conspicuously thick bill. The bill gives it a somewhat raptor-like appearance, but it is not a bird of prey.
sections.habitat: Across sub-Saharan Africa it occurs in moist forest, miombo woodland, riverine forest and wooded savanna. In West Africa, breeding records are strongly associated with closed-canopy forest used by helmetshrike hosts, so habitat association varies across the range.
sections.diet: It mainly eats large insects, including caterpillars, grasshoppers and mantids. It does much of its foraging in the tree canopy.
sections.behavior: The species is an elusive woodland cuckoo; some southern African accounts report local seasonal movements. Its thick bill and build create a hawk-like silhouette, but its ecology is that of a cuckoo.
sections.reproduction: It lays eggs in helmetshrike nests, most often those of the red-billed helmetshrike in southern Africa. The host incubates and raises the cuckoo chick; host use and breeding details differ geographically.
sections.ecology: As a specialized brood parasite, it depends on helmetshrikes and the wooded habitats where they nest. Its insect diet also links it to canopy invertebrate communities; local research reports substantial effects of parasitism on host nesting success.
sections.conservation: Oiseaux.net displays Least Concern on its IUCN status graphic, but its accessible page does not identify the assessment year. Southern African accounts note miombo clearance and fragmentation as concerns; these regional pressures alone do not establish a current global population trend.
